3 KINDS OF CELLS
2016
2015
In a fraction of
a second, an octopus
can change its skin
color, its pattern,
and even its texture.
It can look like
swaying seaweed, a mossy
rock, or a lump
of coral so well
that a diver can
swim right past.
How does it do that?
This relies on three
kinds of cells in the skin.
On top are chromatophores:
small, elastic sacs of
black, brown, red,
orange, or yellow pigment,
each ringed by tiny muscles.
Beneath them lie
iridophores, which work
like living mirrors and
reflect shimmering blues,
greens, and golds.
Deeper still are
leucophores, which scatter
light and add bright
white patches.
Many animals change color
slowly.
Cephalopod camouflage is
wired directly into the
nervous system.
When the brain decides
to change color,
nerve signals travel to
the muscles around each
chromatophore.
Thousands of pigment sacs
expand and contract
together, a bit like
the pixels on a screen.
Color alone rarely fools
a sharp-eyed predator,
so the octopus also
changes the shape of its skin.
Using muscles that raise
small bumps called papillae,
it can push the
skin up into spikes
or ridges in a
fraction of a second,
matching the rough texture
of rocks or algae.
Here is the puzzle.
Most octopuses appear to
be colorblind.
Their eyes have only
one type of light-sensitive
pigment, which in most
animals means no color vision.
Yet an octopus matches
the colors around it
very well.
Scientists have debated
this for a long time.
One idea, published in
2016, is a hypothesis
based on computer models,
and it has not
been confirmed by experiments.
It suggests that the
odd U-shaped pupils of
cuttlefish and squid may
take advantage of chromatic
aberration.
Different colors of light
focus at slightly different
depths, so a shifting
focus might reveal color.
Researchers also found
something surprising.
In 2015, a team
reported that the skin
of the California two-spot
octopus contains opsins,
the light-sensitive proteins
found in eyes.
Patches of skin responded
to light in lab tests.
The skin may sense
light on its own,
although scientists are
still working out how
important this is.
So the octopus is
a master of disguise,
and the science behind
it still holds open questions.

this alien mind,
watch the full video
